real: Write down your findings in the plan file as plans that may be worth trying in future, and update the next plans.
prev_agent: For this kernel, the real latency-hiding mechanisms are fairly limited, and your own profiling already points to the main one. The current `(1,8,2,8,2)` loop in [hip_kernel_fp16.cu](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/kernel/hip/hip_kernel_fp16.cu#L245) is serialized as `compute -> barrier -> refill -> barrier`, so it exposes global refill almost completely. That matches the profiling summary in [HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md#L46), which shows `Sync ~46.7%`, large `s_waitcnt vmcnt(*)`, and concludes there is “effectively no overlap” between refill and WMMA [HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md#L64). The mechanisms that can hide global->LDS latency are: 1. Occupancy across independent waves/workgroups. On gfx1151, the scheduler hides VMEM latency by running other ready waves while one wave waits. The occupancy model is summarized in [GFX1151_REFERENCE.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/GFX1151_REFERENCE.md#L18). For this config, your plan already records `VGPR=184`, `LDS=24576 B` [HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md#L106), which works out to about `50%` occupancy and is VGPR-limited, not LDS-limited. This helps, but barriers blunt it because all 8 waves in the workgroup stop together. 2. Software pipelining across K-chunks. This is the main mechanism that matters here. Issue next-chunk global loads early, let them sit in flight under `vmcnt`, do current-chunk WMMA, then wait only when the next chunk is actually needed. That is exactly what your P3 item says to pursue in [HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md#L125). In practice this comes in three forms: - Register prefetch of the next chunk, then LDS store later. - Ping-pong LDS stages. - Partial/B-only prefetch, because your own ablation shows B refill dominates: `16 KB` per chunk for B vs `8 KB` for A [HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/doc/HIP_OPTIMIZATION_PLAN_FP16.md#L74). For this config, B-first overlap is the highest-value target. 3. Wave specialization / split ownership. A subset of waves performs refill while other waves keep computing, and the scheduler overlaps them at wave granularity. Your kernel already uses a mild version on A via WSGR ownership [hip_kernel_fp16.cu](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/kernel/hip/hip_kernel_fp16.cu#L96), but because refill still happens after a full-workgroup barrier [hip_kernel_fp16.cu](/home/user_aeefbb67/ComfyUI-FeatherOps/kernel/hip/hip_kernel_fp16.cu#L251), that currently reduces load traffic more than it hides latency. If you pipeline the schedule, wave specialization becomes a real latency-hiding tool. 4. Direct global->LDS instructions. RDNA docs do acknowledge that some loads can go from memory directly into LDS [rdna35_instruction_set_architecture.md](/home/user_aeefbb67/rdna35-isa-markdown/rdna35_instruction_set_architecture.md#L4711). CK’s direct-load abstraction describes the useful constraints clearly: each lane moves exactly one DWORD, lanes in a wave must write consecutive DWORDs to LDS, and completion is tracked by `vmcnt`, not `lgkmcnt` [thread_group_tensor_slice_transfer_direct_load.hpp](/home/user_aeefbb67/rocm-libraries/projects/composablekernel/include/ck/tensor_operation/gpu/block/thread_group_tensor_slice_transfer_direct_load.hpp#L15). The problem is practicality on `gfx1151`: - The older async-to-LDS intrinsics are documented as `gfx9/gfx10` only [ROCDLOps.td](/home/user_aeefbb67/amd-llvm-project/mlir/include/mlir/Dialect/LLVMIR/ROCDLOps.td#L1725). - The newer `global.load.async.to.lds.b{8,32,64,128}` path is `gfx1250+` only [ROCDLOps.td](/home/user_aeefbb67/amd-llvm-project/mlir/include/mlir/Dialect/LLVMIR/ROCDLOps.td#L1800). - LLVM MC explicitly marks […]
